newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberian gunmen free rival militia commanders.
newsitem.headline: Liberian gunmen free rival militia commanders.

text.p: Liberian gunmen freed two hostage commanders of a rival faction of Wednesday, a day after they were kidnapped during a U.N.-sponsored ceasefire monitoring mission.

George Boley, head of the Liberia Peace Council -- an ethnic Krahn militia group -- led a mission to tell his own men to release General John Tarnue and General Francis Dolo of the National Patriotic Front of Liberia.

"I am sorry Gentlemen. I didn't order it (the kidnapping)," Boley told the two generals after bringing them to the capital Monrovia and turning them over to U.N. observers and U.S. embassy representatives, witnesses said.
The abduction of the two generals on Tuesday posed a new threat to Liberia's latest peace deal.
Tarnue had bruises on his head and body and a blackened eye which he said were from torture.

A reporter who travelled on the helicopter with U.N. officials and West African diplomats said the two generals were found sitting in front of a house in the southeastern town of Zwedru, with some of their armed captors standing by.
"We have set them free because we only wanted to prove to the international community that we control this place," one Liberia Peace Council gunman was quoted as saying.
Earlier the commander of the West African ECOMOG force, which also took part in the mission that ended in the hostagetaking, ordered the immediate release of the two men.
General Victor Malu, commander of the Nigerian-led force, also demanded the return of property seized from other members of the ceasefire monitoring team to southeast Liberia.
"This act on the part of the LPC is a gross violation of the Abuja Accord," Malu told reporters after talks on Wednesday among peacekeepers, U.N. and faction representatives.
U.N. special envoy Anthony Nyakyi of Tanzania described the seizure as "a serious threat to the peace process".
The two men are supporters of Charles Taylor, the man who launched the civil war in December 1989. The factions have traded allegations of truce violations in the south east.

A Western diplomat who travelled with the truce monitoring team told reporters quick action was necessary to prevent the incident derailing the latest peace deal, which West African leaders brokered in Nigeria's capital Abuja in August.
The peace deal, backed up by the threat of individual sanctions against any faction leader undermining the process, envisages disarmament by January and elections in May.

The war has killed well over 150,000 people. The truce followed fighting that killed hundreds of people in Monrovia in April and May. The United States sent in Marines to protect its embassy and airlifted out U.S. and other foreign nationals.
